summary: Notes by R. W. Watson on a Network Working Group meeting in Urbana, Illinois, 17 February 1971. It was updated by RFC 108 and RFC 123.

eli5.summary: Notes from a meeting held in a town in Illinois.

questions: what was decided at the february 1971 nwg meeting
what was the logger protocol in 1971
subtitle: Richard Watson's notes on a February 1971 Network Working Group meeting, from site status reports to the first committees.

tldr.problem: In early 1971 the sites joining the ARPANET needed to compare progress, settle an interim logger protocol and decide who would work on the open problems.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Working Group met in Urbana, Illinois, heard site reports, adopted the RFC 66 logger protocol with a correction and formed committees on host-host, typewriter connection, data management and sockets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 101 records what was said and decided. It is a meeting record rather than a specification, and it was later updated by RFC 108 and RFC 123.

facts.label: Logger character format
facts.value: 7-bit ASCII in an 8-bit field, eighth bit 0

sections.title: The Urbana Meeting
sections.content:
This RFC, by Richard W. Watson of SRI-ARC, records the Network Working Group (NWG) meeting held in Urbana, Illinois, from Wednesday evening, February 17, to Friday, February 19, 1971. Mike Sher opened by noting that ILLIAC IV was expected to be running that summer. Steve Crocker then asked for topics.

Attendees reported experience. SRI described using the Utah PDP-10 to help move from an XDS 940 to a PDP-10, with round-trip character delays of 4 seconds not uncommon. UCSB and RAND described early experiments with their NCPs, and UCSB's NCP was about 39K bytes. Observers from the Canadian government and IBM also spoke.
sections.eli5: People from many places met in a town in Illinois. They told stories about trying to make their computers talk to each other.

sections.title: Site Status Reports
sections.content:
On Thursday morning each site reported on its network control program (NCP), the software that lets a host use the network. BBN said 15 IMPs were then connected and described a 316 IMP and a terminal interface processor (TIMP) that could handle up to 64 terminals. Other sites, including SDC, Case Western Reserve, Harvard, MIT, Utah, Lincoln Laboratory, UCSB, RAND and UCLA, gave expected dates for getting their NCPs working, ranging from weeks to a few months.

Alex McKenzie of BBN prepared a status form, filled in by site representatives that evening, and BBN and the NIC were to prepare a procedure for keeping that information up to date.
sections.eli5: Each team said how close it was to having its computer ready to join the network, like kids saying how far along their science projects were.

sections.title: Protocol Decisions and Committees
sections.content:
Tom Skinner of Multics opened the logger protocol discussion. The result was that the logger protocol of RFC 66 was adopted, with the correction that allocate commands be issued after the connection is established. Initial communication to the logger is in 7-bit ASCII in an 8-bit field, and the eighth bit should be 0.

Steve Crocker listed known host-host protocol problems: echo, message type, interrupts, marking-padding, and half versus full duplex while establishing a socket. A committee chaired by S. Crocker was appointed to consider them. A typewriter connection protocol committee chaired by Tom O'Sullivan took up character set, end of line, interrupts, message format and duplex. A committee chaired by J. Heafner was to write up issues about socket number structure. Link number 223 was first assigned for UCLA measurements, then link 191 was chosen instead when 223 turned out to be taken.
sections.eli5: They picked one set of rules for logging in, then split into small teams, each in charge of fixing one kind of problem.

sections.title: The NIC and Next Steps
sections.content:
Dick Watson reviewed the Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI, which works through a Station Agent and a Network Liaison person at each site. Planned online services included access to a typewriter version of the On-Line System (NLS), a message service and the NIC catalog. The group also discussed privacy when conversations are filed, microfilm for storing documents, file transfer by name, and accounting.

On the last question, the general consensus was that the meeting was useful but that more preparation should be done ahead of time. People with topics were asked to distribute position papers about a month before the next meeting, if possible.
sections.eli5: One office kept the papers and notes everyone wrote. At the end people agreed the next meeting would go better if everyone prepared first.
